1. Nancy is meeting Paul Caruso, a web designer from a company called Glitch, to discuss creating a website for the concert.

Hello. Thanks for coming today, Paul.
I’m Nancy Chow.
We spoke on the phone.
Hi Nancy. Nice to meet you.
Right well, thanks for agreeing to design the website for our concert.
It’s my pleasure.
We're really looking for something quite simple at this stage.
OK, not a problem.
What's the name of this concert, by the way?
It’s called Music: A Night to Remember OK.
Music: A Night to Remember Right.
OK, what we'd normally have on a page like this is, like, the basic details that you want the public to know about.
Like, say, when the concert will take place.
OK, well, it'll be held on November the 24th.
November the 24th, this year, I presume.
Yeah, 2015. And the location?
Where will it be?
at the Central Theatre of the Hong Kong Cultural Centre.
OK. And the time?
When will it start?
It'll start at half past seven.
So from 7: thirty to 9: thirty pm.
Oh, another thing there is no interval!
If you could mention that on the website!
So no interval!
Ill make that clear.
And who can participate?
Well, young people between the ages of 13 and 18 can participate.
And they should either belong to a school group or an independent group.
So just groups?
No, no, solo participants are welcome too.
What types of performance are you looking for?
What kind of music are they allowed to perform?
Well, it can be jazz bands, rap groups, or even rock music.
OK. how about dance groups?
No, unfortunately, we won't be accepting dance groups just music groups.
And how do they apply?
Well, they should send in a video.
And the video should contain three things.
OK, three things.
Yeah, first it should contain a short video of the artists introducing themselves.
Second, it should have a video of a performance.
And what was the third thing?
Oh yeah, it should contain a video of them telling a funny story about what happened to them when they were performing.
Alright. How can the public get their tickets?
How can they contact you?
Have you got it set up online or Well, we've got four ways for people to buy tickets.
Right. First, they should be able to buy tickets online by clicking on a link or an icon in the shape of a shopping trolley.
OK, a link or an icon in the shape of a shopping trolley.
Secondly, they can call this number 749 -481 -61.
did you get it down?
correct? Yes, that’s correct.
Thirdly, they can send us an email at information at C -A -F dot org That’s O -R -G.
OK, the email address is information at C -A -F dot org Great, Plus, they can get tickets at the box office.
Alright, I think I have most of the important information for now.
Just a couple of questions about the look of the webpage.
OK, Let me show you some designs for a logo we've used for this type of event before.
We can adapt these a bit obviously.
So which of these four do you think would be the best for the show?
OK, let me see.
well, I don’t want the one with the brake dancers as I said, it’s a music concert.
So that one’s out.
um, I’m not sure about the one with the guitar.
It gives the impression that we're only looking for serious musicians and not singers.
Right, what about the other two?
Well, either of these would do but I think I'd go for this one.
Just because it’s a bunch of people together as opposed to just one girl.
OK and what would you like the background colour of this website to be?

But it might be difficult to read the words if the background’s red.
Yeah, that’s true.
You know what, I think just a simple white background will do with black or maybe dark blue writing.
Great. rate. I can show you a temporary version of the website by next week.
And if you like it, we can meet again to discuss adding more information to the website.
Thank you very much, Paul!
I appreciate it!
You're welcome. See you next week.
That is the end of Task 1.

another thing I'd thought of was related to the audience.

We want people to come and have a good time.

Is the type of music too strange?
If it’s too strange, they might not like it.
Yeah, but even if the audience doesn’t like the music, it could still be really educational for them.
And we should definitely be considering that.
Don’t you think?
You know, it's good to be exposed to new types of music.
It’s important for people to hear something new.
They can learn more about different types of music.
Fine. Fair enough.

If they write their own original music.

to play pop songs!

Task 4. Nancy is appearing on a radio show called Power Focus along with Dr.
Wendy Craig from The Hong Kong Chamber Orchestra, Listen to the show and answer the questions below.

OK, welcome to Power Focus Hong Kong's number one radio debate show.
My name is John Barnes and I, am your host.
Tonight we have with us Nancy Chow from the Hong Kong Cultural Arts Foundation and one of the judges on Belavoche, the latest music reality show to hit our screens and Dr.
Wendy Craig from the Hong Kong Chamber Orchestra.
The motion in front of us tonight is related to music reality shows and goes as follows.
Music Reality Shows are killing the music industry.
industry. For a change, tonight we'll start with arguments against the motion.
Nancy, you have two minutes to argue against the motion.
OK. Thank you, John.
I have three points to make to convince you that music reality shows are not destroying music.
The first is that these shows provide young people with the way to hear great pop music.
I know, I know, I am sure we would all love young people to be listening to far deeper music than most pop music.
But if young people are listening to pop music at least they are listening to something.
It is important for young people to develop a love for music and the best place to start is pop music, And where is it that young people hear good pop music?
In music reality shows like ours, Secondly, to say that this type of program is destroying the industry is false.
It has often been said by opponents of these shows that they stop other artists from getting a chance to have a successful career.
However, this seems to be a very pessimistic view of the music industry.
In fact, the music industry has always been rich in its variety, from hip hop to folk, and rock.
Many artists are still successful despite these programs existing.
My third point is that programs like the Voice of China can actually provide information about singing techniques that you have to learn if you want to be a better singer.
In other words, a singer may have talent but they still need training These shows are also a good way of dispelling the myth that talented singers don’t have to work hard.
The shows are great at showing that being a singer requires a lot of practice in order to improve.
So I would say these programmes are not destroying music.
They are one of the reasons that music is still flourishing.
OK, thanks Nancy.
Now Dr. Craig, you have two minutes to argue for the motion.
I’m sorry Nancy but I firmly believe that shows like the Voice of China are contributors to the slaughter of the music industry.
And I also have three points to support my stance.
First, let us be honest here for a minute, reality music shows may be entertaining but what these shows offer is not high quality music.

It is instead what might be called televised karaoke I call it televised karaoke for two reasons: Firstly it’s televised karaoke because we get our enjoyment from seeing how bad a contestant is singing

rather than enjoying how well a singer's doing The second reason is that, even when they, the contestants, the contestants are doing well, they're doing well by copying famous artists not through being original.
My second point supporting the motion is related to what happens after the end of the series.
The winners of such TV series achieve instant fame so they suddenly become as famous as many more established singers.
This is simply unfair.
It creates an unfair market where other singers don’t get as much publicity as the winner of the reality show.
Haven't these other singers work just as hard?
I think I've got time to make one final point, My final point is that these shows sell a lie.
The lie is that success is easy in the music industry.
The true effort needed to succeed in the music industry is being lost, cost, because it seems so easy that everyone can do it, and success can happen overnight.
In the vast majority of cases success does not happen overnight.
It often takes years and years of hard work and new musicians need to know that.
And the worst thing is that the consequence of perpetuating this lie is that many musicians won't keep going when things start getting tough.
Many musicians will simply give up.
OK, thanks to Nancy and Wendy.
Well we went into the streets of Hong Kong to get people's opinions on this.
Speedy Chan reports.
That is the end of Task 4.
